core: the working definition of capital budgeting: the process of evaluating and selecting long-term investments
why the process exists: big, long-lived decisions deserve structured analysis before money is committed
the five steps of the process: identify opportunities, estimate cash flows, evaluate, choose, review
the three named evaluation tools: payback period, net present value, internal rate of return
the discount-rate question: future cash flows are discounted at the firm's cost of capital
risk in the process: uncertainty about future cash flows
the honest framing: capital budgeting is disciplined guessing about the future
supporting: examples of capital projects: factories, equipment, new markets, workforce expansion, product R&D
investment appraisal as an alternative name for the process (Investopedia)
cash-flow estimation and timing as the raw material the evaluation tools work on
incremental cash flows and sunk costs as a consideration in fair evaluation (CFI)
outOfScope: NPV mechanics and calculations (sibling topic: finance:foundations:net-present-value)
cost-of-capital definition and calculation, including WACC (sibling topic: finance:foundations:cost-of-capital)
cash-flow statement preparation and estimation depth (sibling topic: finance:foundations:cash-flow)
profitability index, discounted payback, and MIRR (alternative-method depth)
any formulas beyond naming what each tool measures

claims.claim: Working definition: capital budgeting is the process companies use to evaluate proposed major projects or investments by analyzing their expected cash inflows and outflows (Investopedia); CFI frames it as the decision-making process companies follow for choosing which capital-intensive projects to pursue; OpenStax frames it as deciding whether spending money today will make money in the future.

Capital budgeting decisions concern large, long-lived investments: opening a new factory, buying major equipment, entering a new market, significant workforce expansion, research and development of new products, or taking a significant stake in an outside venture.

The core argument for the process: to grow and remain competitive, a firm relies on new products, improved products, and new markets, and these ventures require money spent now against cash flows that arrive over many years, so the firm must judge whether a project will generate enough cash to cover its initial cost and add value.

The capital budgeting process can be summarized in five steps: identify candidate opportunities, estimate each project's expected cash flows, evaluate the projects with the firm's tools, choose which to fund, and review results after the project is running. The sources describe the cash-flow estimation and evaluation stages explicitly; the five-step ordering is this lesson's synthesis of the standard process.

Payback period is the simplest project evaluation tool: it measures how long it takes a project to recover its initial investment in cash flow. Its usefulness is limited because it ignores the time value of money.

Net present value (NPV) is the gap between the today-value of a project's expected cash inflows and the present value of its cash outflows; a project should be accepted when NPV is positive, because it is expected to add value measured in today's dollars, and rejected when NPV is negative.

Internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate that sets the present value of a project's expected cash inflows exactly equal to the present value of its outflows (the rate at which NPV equals zero); a project should be accepted when its IRR is greater than the firm's cost of attracting capital, and rejected when it is lower.

The discount-rate question: future cash flows cannot be compared directly with today's spending, so they are translated into present value using a discount rate; the rate a company uses is its cost of capital, the cost of attracting funds, and CFI notes the discount rate used is often the company's weighted average cost of capital (WACC).

Risk is built into the process: a project's future cash flows are estimates, not promises — customer demand, costs, and the wider economy can all differ from the plan — so the honest framing is that capital budgeting is disciplined guessing about the future.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which evaluation tool should a firm trust?
positions: Payback period is quick and simple but ignores the time value of money and offers no objective accept-or-reject criterion (OpenStax 16.1/16.4).
NPV and IRR both account for the timing of cash flows, and firms commonly use a combination of metrics — IRR, NPV, payback — rather than one tool (CFI).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson names all three tools at literacy level, notes that NPV and IRR are the more complete ones because they account for timing, and points to their own sibling lessons for the mechanics.

conflictingEvidence.issue: NPV and IRR can rank mutually exclusive projects differently.
positions: In OpenStax's Sam's Sporting Goods example, the regular embroidery machine has a lower NPV ($2,835.62) but a higher IRR (14.10%) than the heavy-duty machine (NPV $3,970.67, IRR 13.20%), so ranking by the two methods gives different winners.
OpenStax's stated goal is choosing projects that add value to the company, with NPV estimating how much value a project will create.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The literacy-level lesson does not adjudicate ranking conflicts; it presents NPV as the value-added measure and leaves choosing between competing projects to the sibling net-present-value topic.

The generated draft's framing of capital budgeting as 'a label on a toolbox drawer' — an unsourced metaphor, not a definition.
The generated draft's vocabulary treating 'context' and 'evidence' as key capital budgeting terms — generic, not topic-specific.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Section 16.1: Payback Period Method
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Internet Archive capture (2022-10-06). Supports: payback period as how long it takes to recover the initial investment in cash flow; it is the simplest method; its limitation of ignoring the time value of money.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Section 16.2: Net Present Value (NPV) Method
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Internet Archive capture (2022-09-29). Supports: NPV as present value of inflows minus present value of outflows; accept when positive because the project adds value; the firm's cost of funds (9% in the worked example) as the discount rate; cash flows translated into present value because they occur in different time periods.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Section 16.3: Internal Rate of Return (IRR) Method
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Internet Archive capture (2022-09-29). Supports: IRR as the discount rate that sets present value of inflows equal to present value of outflows (NPV equal to zero); accept if IRR exceeds the firm's cost of attracting capital, reject if below.
